INVE Raises $300K Pre-Seed for Saudi Event Tech [2026]
Dr. Elena Marchetti
Updated Oct 22, 2026 · 15 min read
Saudi event-tech startup INVE raised US$300,000 in pre-seed funding from Outliers Venture Capital, with the round announced on October 22, 2026, according to reports from waya.media, EU-Startups, Tech in Asia, Disrupt Africa and Tech.eu. The company sells personalised invitations and event-management tools to both consumers and businesses. It was founded in 2024 by Abdulrahman Alabdulkarim, who is identified as its founder and CEO.

The cheque is small. It is roughly a tenth of the $3M that Reduck secured this month for AI agent web automation . Still, the story has a detail that larger rounds rarely offer: the lead investor was the startup’s first paid business customer before it wrote a cheque. That sequence says more about product-market fit than most pitch decks do.
The money will go toward expanding INVE’s business platform and growing its consumer product beyond weddings. The business platform only launched in August 2026, so the company is funding a product that launched in August 2026 and is still being introduced to more companies. This analysis walks through what is confirmed, what the platform does, why the engineering behind a digital invitation is harder than it looks, and where the open questions sit.

articles.text:
Fundraise Oct 26, 2026, 16:33 UTC
UVU-linked startup Deload raises seed round for AI personal-training platform
What's the deal? Deload, a startup building an AI-powered platform for independent personal trainers, has raised a seed round from Startup Ignition Ventures Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , the company announced in October. Terms were not disclosed.
What's the endgame? Deload consolidates training-plan generation, workout management, client check-ins, and payments into one platform. Its AI drafts programs spanning 12 to 16 weeks, which the trainer reviews, approves, and customizes — the trainer remains the "coach of record."
How it works. The workflow begins with a trainer's approach and a client's intake information. "Your approach. Their intake. Deload drafts the plan. You approve it," the company says. Trainers can then edit sessions in plain English, with downstream weeks adjusting automatically.
Why now? Both founders, Sean Frasure and Ethan Rasmussen, came through Utah Valley University's Sandbox entrepreneurship program and the Startup Ignition Bootcamp. The company — rebranded from Revyl — placed third at UVU's ZinnStarter pitch competition in April 2026.
What could go wrong? Deload is entering a market with established competitors including Trainerize Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , Everfit Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , and TrueCoach Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → . Convincing trainers to switch is hard: existing customers have years of client data and routines tied to their current software. The founders are building a migration tool, but its effectiveness at scale is unproven.
The signal: The round reflects growing interest in tech-enabled coaching. Gyms including Vasa Fitness Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , New York Sports Club, and HOTWORX rolled out AI training tools in 2026, and UK-based MAGIC AI Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → raised $11 million in September to expand its AI fitness mirror in the US. For now, Deload is an early entrant betting that AI built into the workflow — not bolted on as a feature — is enough to win over independent trainers.

articles.text:
Fundraise Oct 27, 2026, 14:46 UTC
AI forecaster Prophetlab raises tens of millions of yuan in seed round
What's the deal? Prophetlab, an AI prediction engine startup founded less than four months ago, has closed a seed round of tens of millions of yuan, with backing from investors including Ivy Capital Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → . The company says it has also secured commercial orders worth several million yuan.
What's the endgame? Prophetlab builds Prophet Engine, a forecasting system that reached the top of the FutureX overall rankings published by ByteDance Seed . Early projects used large AI models to predict World Cup outcomes, correctly forecasting the final result and the top four teams, with some models hitting roughly 75% accuracy.
Who's behind it? The team is made up of AI PhDs and fintech master's graduates. Founding members worked on training billion-scale models for Alibaba's Qianwen Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → and Tencent's Hunyuan , and the company collaborates with Professor Yan Junchi's team at Shanghai Jiao Tong University.
Why now? AI forecasting is becoming a visible startup category, with recent reports saying systems are approaching top human forecasters on benchmarks. In September, UK startup Mantic Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → raised $25 million in seed funding to build enterprise forecasting tools.
What could go wrong? A single leaderboard result and claimed World Cup predictions do not yet prove reliability across business use cases. The open question is whether Prophetlab can turn benchmark wins into repeatable, calibrated forecasts that customers will pay for.
The signal: Prophetlab's next move is the Investor's Last Exam rankings, aimed squarely at commercial predictions. That focus shows where the category is heading: from demos and sports bets toward forecasts enterprises will actually buy.

Physical AI startup Tensrai raises Rs 3.4 Cr in pre-seed round
Hyderabad-based Physical AI startup Tensrai has raised Rs 3.4 crore in a pre-seed funding from India Accelerator, Finvolve, Hyderabad Angels and other angels.
The fresh capital will be used to accelerate technology development, strengthen

Follow Us
New Update
Hyderabad-based Physical AI startup Tensrai has raised Rs 3.4 crore in a pre-seed funding from India Accelerator, Finvolve, Hyderabad Angels and other angels.
The fresh capital will be used to accelerate technology development, strengthen engineering and deployment capabilities, and support expansion into domestic and international markets, Tensrai said in a press release.
Co-founded by Sai Nikhil Rao Gona, Venkata Sai Charan Chalamalasetty, Harshith Uppalapati, and Vivek Datta, Tensrai is developing a unified, retrofittable autonomy platform that enables industrial and commercial robots, vehicles and machines to perform physical tasks autonomously.
The platform combines vision-first navigation, AI-based localisation, vision-language model (VLM)-powered reasoning, autonomous mobility, robotic arm manipulation and vision-language-action (VLA)-based teach-and-deploy capabilities. The technology is designed to help machines perceive their surroundings, reason through tasks, learn skills and execute operations with limited human intervention.
Tensrai aims to bring autonomous capabilities to both purpose-built machines and existing equipment through retrofitting, potentially reducing the cost and complexity of adopting robotics across industrial and commercial settings.
The startup is targeting applications such as autonomous material handling and cleaning across factories, warehouses, airports, hospitals, shopping malls and commercial campuses. It is also developing a general-purpose mobile manipulator that combines autonomous mobility with robotic arms to perform tasks across material handling, cleaning, manufacturing and construction.
Tensrai plans to generate revenue through multiple streams, including robot sales, autonomy retrofitting, Robot-as-a-Service (RaaS) and customised solutions. It also plans to expand into international markets.
The funding comes amid growing interest in Physical AI, which combines artificial intelligence with robotic systems and machines to enable them to understand and interact with the physical world. Unlike software-based AI applications, Physical AI systems are designed to translate perception and reasoning into real-world actions.
With a common autonomy platform for different types of machines, Tensrai aims to help businesses automate repetitive, labour-intensive and operationally complex tasks across industrial and commercial settings.
